title: Small samples do not make pooled pricing safe
shortTitle: No safe pooled price in small samples
oneLine: Under the regularity conditions of Xie, Zhu and Shishkin (2025), no range of small sample sizes guarantees that one pooled empirical price beats segmented empirical pricing, for any number of markets.
abstract: A seller with a small sample of past buyers can post one price chosen from the whole sample (pooled empirical revenue maximisation) or split buyers into markets by a covariate and price each market separately. Xie, Zhu and Shishkin (Theoretical Economics, 2025) showed that segmentation learns more slowly and asked whether there is a finite range of sample sizes, with lower endpoint at least three, on which pooled pricing beats every segmented rule for every distribution in their regularity class. This candidate shows that the regularity conditions alone do not guarantee such a range. For every number of markets K and every finite upper sample size N, one atomless distribution satisfying the conditions makes K-market pricing (with empty markets priced at the pooled price) strictly more profitable at every sample size from 2 to N, with an explicit positive bound. Combined with a distribution on which segmentation wins in large samples, this gives two fixed distributions in one fixed regularity class that defeat pooled dominance at every sample size; for two markets the threshold is explicit. The mechanism is a rare high-value segment: one high observation pulls a pooled price up and loses ordinary buyers. The provable constructions use extreme constants and tiny gains; an exploratory simulation shows relative gains up to about ten per cent at moderate parameters. The question with moderate constants fixed in advance remains open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: For every number of equal-length markets K ≥ 2 and every N ≥ 2, one atomless law satisfying Assumption 2 of Xie, Zhu and Shishkin makes K-market ERM beat pooled ERM at every n = 2,…,N, by at least 7qa/512 with a = 1/(256N⁴), q = a/(128N) (Theorem 1, proof with exact certificates).

For each K, two fixed laws in one regularity class, and in every more permissive class, defeat pooled dominance at every n ≥ 2; for K = 2 the threshold N* = 916,723,536 is explicit (Corollary 4, proof).
Empty markets receive the pooled price, the convention of the source's two-sample discussion; the construction depends on it.
In a simulation of the unsmoothed model at moderate parameters, two-market ERM wins at every n = 3,…,40 in eight of nine settings, with relative gains up to about 10% (Section 4, numerical).
Open: whether a dominance window exists when moderate regularity constants are fixed in advance.

narration: Small samples do not make pooled pricing safe. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the question. A seller who has seen a few past customers can either set one price for everyone, chosen to maximise revenue on the whole sample, or split customers into groups, for example by region, and choose a separate price for each group. Splitting leaves fewer observations per group, so with very little data the single pooled price seems the safer choice. A 2025 paper in Theoretical Economics showed that splitting does learn more slowly, and asked whether, under standard smoothness conditions, pooling is guaranteed to win at small sample sizes. The main finding is that it is not. Imagine many ordinary customers with low valuations and a rare group willing to pay much more. When the sample happens to contain one of those rare customers, the pooled price can be pulled up towards that one valuation, and most ordinary customers stop buying. Splitting the data keeps that observation out of the ordinary group's price. The paper tunes the frequencies so that this protection outweighs every cost of splitting, at every sample size in any chosen range and for any number of groups, and it builds a fixed pair of demand models that defeats pooling at every sample size. The limits: the proven examples use extreme parameters with tiny gains, a simulation suggests gains of a few per cent at moderate parameters but is not a proof, the result depends on how empty groups are priced, and the version with moderate assumptions fixed in advance is still open. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, checked by AI-assisted review only, not peer review. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
